name: Okara
tagline: An AI assistant product at okara.ai; the public detail on exact scope and pricing is thin, so treat the specifics here as unverified.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: We do not have verified detail on exactly what Okara does or what it charges, and we are not going to invent either. So take this as a placeholder verdict for the shape of product it appears to be: an AI assistant layered over your own documents and notes. That shape is a weekend build with an API key, a local vector index, and a chat pane, and the core value genuinely survives self-hosting. What does not survive is the boring half: mobile, sync, auth, and the couple hundred small decisions that make a tool pleasant instead of a demo. If the real product turns out to rest on proprietary data or a model nobody else can call, this drops to no.
coreLoopDIY: Runs a local web app that ingests your files, indexes them, and answers questions and drafts text against them through an LLM API key you own.
requirements: An OpenAI-compatible API key (or a local model via Ollama)
Node 20 and a machine you are willing to leave running
Your own documents in a folder, since there are no connectors
whatYouLose: Any mobile or desktop client, this is a browser tab on localhost
Hosted sync across devices, and the auth layer that would make that safe
Prebuilt connectors to Drive, Notion, Slack or whatever they actually integrate with
Someone else's prompt tuning and retrieval tricks, which is most of the perceived quality
A support inbox and a roadmap that is not you on a Sunday
moatNotes: For assistant products the defensible part is almost never the model call, it is retrieval quality and the integrations that fill the index without the user doing chores.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for assistants because the setup cost is where motivation dies. A self-hosted version means you own the ingestion pipeline, the embedding bill, the chunking decisions, and every regression when a dependency shifts. A paid product hands you a working index five minutes after signup, on your phone, with your work accounts already connected, and quietly improves retrieval while you get on with your job. That gap is small in capability and large in friction, which is exactly the gap subscriptions are priced into.
notes: Filed on thin public information: the verdict is about the category, not a close read of this specific product.
prompt:
Build a local-only AI assistant over my own files. No accounts, no cloud services, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- TypeScript, Next.js App Router, single app, run with `npm run dev`.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for documents, chunks, chats and messages.
- sqlite-vec (or a plain float32 blob column plus in-memory cosine search if that is simpler) for vector similarity.
- Tailwind for styling. No component library.
- LLM and embedding calls go to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Read OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_BASE_URL from .env.local. Ship .env.example, never commit real keys.

What it does:
1. A Sources page where I point at a local folder path. Walk it, parse .md, .txt and .pdf (use pdf-parse), chunk to roughly 800 tokens with 100 token overlap, embed, store. Show per-file status and re-index on demand only, no watchers.
2. A Chat page: threaded conversations stored in SQLite. On each turn, embed the question, pull the top 8 chunks, build a grounded prompt, stream the answer back with server-sent events.
3. Every answer shows its cited chunks with file name and a snippet, expandable. If retrieval scores are all weak, say so instead of guessing.
4. A Drafts mode: same retrieval, but the prompt asks for a written passage in a chosen tone rather than an answer.
5. Full-text keyword search across chunks as a fallback tab, using SQLite FTS5.

Explicitly out of scope: multi-user auth, third-party connectors, mobile app, background jobs, Docker, payments, analytics.

Deliver a README with setup in under ten lines, seed a tiny sample docs folder so the first run has something to index, and keep the whole thing under roughly 1500 lines. Working over clever.
